catalog_quote: [Pulipaty 2019] The elusive nature of Telugu stress ... Previous works on Telugu word stress (Sitapati 1936; Sailaja 1985) postulate: Primary stress falls on the first syllable; But if the first syllable is light and the second heavy, it falls on the second syllable. However, a study on auditory perception of Telugu stress by Lisker and Krishnamurti (1991) finds contradictory results: Little consistency in stress judgements of speakers; A somewhat noticeable pattern is that the second syllable carries stress; The first syllable stressed only if it contained a long vowel and if the second syllable contained a short vowel ... This suggests that, although native speaker intuitions about stress are weak, metrical structure plays a significant role in determining phonological alternations in Telugu. || [Bhaskararao & Ray 2017, Suprasegmentals] Telugu does not have lexically contrastive stres…

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes on all three locators. The classification (weight-hedged, left-edge two-syllable window, default initial) rests on a 2019 AMP poster carrying Sitapati 1936/Sailaja 1985/Kolachina 2016 second-hand; the held primaries (K&G 1985 reference grammar, JIPA 2017, SPA 1979, and now Lisker 1963) are silent on stress position or deny only contrastive stress. The newly fetched sources Lisker & Krishnamurti 1991 (first-hand, replacing the poster's paraphrase) refines rather than overturns: it confirms 'no contrastive stress', reports no initial preference, a penult/second-syllable tendency in all-light trisyllables, trochaic all-light disyllables, and a weak preference for the last long vowel, with Telugu listeners near-random - i.e. exactly the contest that motivates the HEDGED verdict; it does not support a categorical left-window rule but also does not establish a different one. Nothing

sources.citation: Lisker, Leigh & Bh. Krishnamurti. 1991. Lexical stress in a 'stressless' language: judgments by Telugu- and English-speaking linguists. Proceedings of the XIIth International Congress of Phonetic Sciences (Aix-en-Provence), vol. 2, 90-93.
sources.quote: Telugu called 'a language without contrastive stress'; Hyman's (1977) survey lists Telugu as 'having dominant initial stress. The basis for this assessment of Telugu seemed doubtful to us'. Results (50 di-/trisyllables, 10 Telugu + 15 English linguists): 'neither showed any strong preference for selecting initial syllables as the bearers of primary stress. If anything, the penultimate syllable was somewhat more often chosen as the locus of primary stress' ... sources.citation: Lisker, Leigh. 1963. Introduction to Spoken Telugu. New York: American Council of Learned Societies (ERIC microfiche, archive.org micro_IA41153010_0926, scanned text).
sources.quote: Only intonation and emphasis: 'In emphatic utterance a word may be given prominence by aspirating the first consonant'; sentence-final syllable under the falling (+) contour 'may also be somewhat prolonged and stressed'. No word-stress position rule (confirms SPA 1979: 'Neither Lisker nor Krishnamurti mentions word accent patterns').
sources.locator: Phonetic preface / Introduction pp. xv-xxiv (scanned lines 1455-1815)

sources.quote: No statement on word stress; paper is about syllabification, SSP violations, codas and orthographic conditioning.

sources.citation: Nagamma Reddy, K. 1999. Vowel and consonant length contrasts in Telugu. Proceedings of ICPhS-14 (San Francisco), 2231-2234.
sources.quote: 'the functions manifested by stress in stress-languages are manifested by length in Telugu'; 'Duration in Telugu functions as stress does across languages'; 'length in word initial segments/syllables too is a marker of emphatic stress in Telugu'. No word-stress position rule.
sources.locator: Abstract; sec. 4 'Functions of length beyond word level', 4.3, 4.7
